title: VoteRing (Raft-style leader election service)

title: FraudScore (transaction fraud detection model)
question: How did you handle the fact that fraud cases were much rarer than normal transactions in your training data?

title: QuickLookup (read-heavy product lookup API)
question: How do you keep the Redis cache from serving stale data after a product is updated?
answer: We invalidate proactively: the write path that updates a product in Postgres publishes an invalidation event with the product ID right after the transaction commits, and every app instance subscribes to that channel and deletes the corresponding Redis key. We deliberately delete rather than update the cache entry, because updating it risks writing stale data if two updates race -- a delete just forces the next read to repopulate from the source of truth. We also keep a short TTL as a safety net in case an invalidation message is ever dropped, so the system self-heals even if the pub/sub layer has a hiccup.
authoring_note: Excellent: correct throughout, explicit reasoning about the update-race hazard (why delete beats update), and a defensive TTL fallback.

title: TaskRunner (background job processing system)
question: What happens if a worker crashes while holding a claimed job?
answer: Every claimed job gets a heartbeat timestamp that the worker refreshes periodically while it's working. A separate reaper process periodically scans for jobs stuck in 'in progress' whose heartbeat is older than a threshold, and resets them back to 'pending' so another worker can pick them up. We made the threshold generous -- a few multiples of the expected job duration -- so a slow-but-alive worker doesn't get its job stolen out from under it, which would risk two workers writing results for the same job.
authoring_note: Excellent: correct heartbeat+reaper crash-recovery mechanism with explicit reasoning about the double-processing risk of an aggressive threshold.

title: EdgeRelay (CDN-style edge routing layer)
question: How does EdgeRelay avoid routing traffic to an edge node that's silently failing?
answer: Health checks alone weren't enough, because a node can pass a lightweight liveness check while still failing real requests under load. So we track a rolling error rate per edge node from actual production traffic, and if it crosses a threshold we pull the node out of rotation even though its health check is still green. Once it's out, we keep sending it a small trickle of shadow traffic so we can tell when it's actually recovered before putting it back, rather than immediately trusting the health check to flip green again.
authoring_note: Excellent: correctly identifies the health-check-vs-real-traffic divergence and a sound error-rate + shadow-traffic mitigation.

title: AuthEdge (JWT/OAuth authentication gateway)
question: Why did you move from storing session tokens in localStorage to httpOnly cookies?
answer: localStorage is readable by any JavaScript running on the page, so a single successful XSS injection anywhere in the app could exfiltrate every user's token. httpOnly cookies aren't accessible to JavaScript at all, which closes that specific theft vector. The trade-off is that cookies are automatically attached to every request to the domain, including ones we didn't intend, which opens up CSRF -- so we paired the change with a SameSite=Strict attribute and a CSRF token on state-changing requests, since httpOnly alone would have traded one vulnerability class for another.
authoring_note: Excellent: correct, nuanced XSS-vs-CSRF trade-off with the specific mitigation pairing.

title: QueryTune (dashboard query optimization)
question: Why didn't adding more indexes to the orders table solve your write throughput problem?
answer: Indexes speed up reads but every additional index has to be updated on every write, so we were trading write throughput for read speed -- exactly the wrong direction for a table that gets far more writes than reads. What actually helped was partitioning the orders table by date, since most of the write load was appends to the current partition and most queries only touched recent partitions anyway, so we avoided the tree depth and page-split costs that were slowing writes down on the single large table.
authoring_note: Excellent: correctly reasons through the index/write tradeoff and lands on the accurate explanation (partitioning) with sound causal reasoning.

title: NotifyHub (fan-out event notification system)
question: How do you guarantee a subscriber doesn't process the same event twice?
answer: We can't fully guarantee exactly-once delivery at the messaging layer -- our queue only guarantees at-least-once, so redelivery can happen after a consumer crash before it acks. Instead we made processing idempotent: every event carries a unique ID, and each subscriber records processed IDs in its own database as part of the same transaction that applies the event's effects. If the same event arrives again, the insert of that ID fails on a uniqueness constraint and the handler treats it as a no-op rather than reapplying the effect. That gets us effectively-once behavior without needing the queue itself to promise it.
authoring_note: Excellent: correctly distinguishes at-least-once delivery from exactly-once processing and gives a real, sound idempotency mechanism.

title: VoteRing (Raft-style leader election service)
question: How do you know a majority of nodes agree before committing a write in VoteRing?
answer: Once the leader gets acknowledgments from more than half the nodes including itself, it considers the write committed and returns success. The acknowledgment just means each follower received the write over the network and applied it to its in-memory state -- we don't wait for followers to flush to disk before acking, since disk writes are slow and the in-memory copies on a majority of nodes are already enough redundancy to protect against losing the data.
authoring_note: The majority-quorum logic itself is correct, but relying on in-memory-only acknowledgment as sufficient durability is a genuine, meaningful misconception (correlated failures can still lose 'committed' data).

title: FraudScore (transaction fraud detection model)
question: Why did you use accuracy as your primary metric when evaluating the fraud model?
answer: Accuracy tells us the overall percentage of transactions we classified correctly, which is the most direct measure of how well the model is doing overall, so I used it as the main number I reported and optimized the threshold against.
authoring_note: A real, well-known misconception for a rare-class problem: accuracy is a poor primary metric for imbalanced fraud detection, stated confidently as if universally sound.

title: StreamPipe (Kafka-based event processing pipeline)
question: How do you make sure events are processed in the exact order they happened?
answer: We just publish every event to the same Kafka topic, and since Kafka is a single ordered log, any consumer reading from that topic will see and process every event in exactly the order it happened, regardless of how many partitions the topic has.
authoring_note: A classic, well-known Kafka misconception: ordering is only guaranteed within a single partition, not across partitions of the same topic.

title: GeoPulse (GPS trail-running tracker app)
question: How does GeoPulse calculate calories burned during a run?
answer: GeoPulse's GPS track can be noisy in urban canyons, so we run a Kalman filter over the raw location updates before using them for anything else. The filter models the runner's position and velocity as state variables and updates its estimate using the phone's accelerometer data between GPS fixes, which smooths out the jumps you'd otherwise see when GPS momentarily loses accuracy near tall buildings. We also discard any GPS fix whose reported horizontal accuracy is worse than 20 meters, since including it would do more harm than good to the filtered track.

title: LedgerVault (SQL ledger service)
question: How do you handle currency conversion for international transactions?
answer: Every transaction request carries a client-generated idempotency key, and before processing we check whether we've already seen that key; if we have, we just return the stored result from the first attempt instead of processing it again. This protects against the client's network retry logic accidentally double-charging someone if the first response got lost in transit.

title: LedgerVault (SQL ledger service)
question: How do you prevent double-processing of the same payment webhook?
answer: Every webhook payload includes the provider's own event ID, and before we process it we try to insert that ID into a 'processed_events' table with a unique constraint on the ID column, inside the same transaction that applies the payment effects. If the insert fails because the ID already exists, we know it's a duplicate delivery and skip processing -- this covers both the provider retrying a webhook after a timeout and us receiving it twice for any other reason.

title: TaskRunner (background job processing system)
question: How do you prevent duplicate job processing while also recovering jobs from crashed workers?
answer: Workers claim jobs with an atomic conditional update that only succeeds for one worker, which prevents duplicate processing at claim time. For crash recovery, every claimed job carries a heartbeat that the worker refreshes while working, and a reaper resets any job whose heartbeat goes stale back to pending so another worker can pick it up.

title: MigrateForge (database schema migration tool)
question: How does MigrateForge apply schema migrations safely in production?
answer: Migrations run inside a transaction wherever the database supports transactional DDL, and the tool computes a checksum of each migration file so a previously-applied migration can't be silently edited and re-run without being caught.
